title: Matt Pollins — Inside the Claude-Native Law Firm (agents.law interview with Zack Shapiro)
author: Matt Pollins · Zack Shapiro

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction

st.t: Agentic infrastructure: Harvey tests vertical vendor durability
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core thesis and adds a concrete AI-native law-firm case: Rains reports using Claude to reduce staffing needs and service costs while experimenting with subscription pricing. It also reinforces the cluster’s constraint that verification and human judgment remain capacity bottlenecks, preventing fully autonomous or unlimited scaling. Its preference for direct foundation-model use additionally sharpens the cluster’s uncertainty about durable vertical-platform advantage.

> > The tension Zack identifies is that the value of the work product is becoming untethered from the hours spent producing it, but the capacity to exercise judgment is still measured in human time.

st.t: Legal economics: AI makes adoption a model problem
st.an: Rains provides a concrete AI-native example of the cluster’s proposition: AI efficiency is paired with lower rates, subscription-oriented pricing and leaner staffing, while human judgment and verification remain binding constraints. This materially develops the synthesis’s pricing, leverage and supervision themes, though the performance claims are Shapiro’s reported experience rather than independent evidence.

kp.k: Direct document manipulation and external memory underpin Claude workflows
kp.d: Shapiro identifies code generation and local-file access as Claude's practical advantages in his legal work. He describes moving from manually applying ChatGPT suggestions in Word to directly generating tracked changes, while markdown files provide reusable context outside a conversation's context window. These are practitioner accounts rather than comparative performance findings.
qs: With Claude, he found a way to get it to manipulate documents directly, which he describes as XML under the hood, published as a Word doc with tracked changes.
Instead of relying on the model's memory and context window, Zack also stores context in markdown files on his computer, effectively creating external memory that can be referenced as needed.

kp.k: Precise instructions and iterative skills encode reusable legal judgment
kp.d: Shapiro argues that prompting and context, rather than additional template training or RAG, are the main bottlenecks in legal AI. He describes encoding successful interactions into reusable Skills and updating them when outputs disappoint. Pollins endorses experimentation with Skills but questions whether every practitioner has the discipline and time for this iterative work.
qs: The bottleneck is the prompting and the context.
Zack describes it as a zip file you could send to 500 associates, your judgment encoded as a skill file that scales like software.
When it does something well, you reinforce it. When it does something poorly, you update the skill.

It's a compelling idea, though it does require a level of discipline and iteration and one wonders if every practitioner will have the time or inclination for that, unless it happens automatically in the background.

kp.k: Everyday drafting shifts into Claude, with accessibility benefits
kp.d: The interview describes engagement-letter preparation moving from manual Word edits to a short instruction. Shapiro also reports using prompts often 2,000 words long for broader work and building a Claude Code–ElevenLabs tool to read long documents aloud because of a health condition. His claim that drudgery has disappeared and work feels more joyful is a personal assessment, not a measured productivity result.
qs: Email is still where the work arrives. But the "substantive lawyering" now happens inside Claude.
Now it's a one-sentence instruction: engagement letter for this company, addressed to this person, here's the retainer, standard scope.
He's also built a custom tool combining Claude Code with ElevenLabs that reads long documents aloud, which is helpful as Zack has a health condition making it hard to read longer documents on screen.
Long prompts, often 2,000 words, written like essays.
Zack says the drudgery is gone and the work feels more joyful.

kp.k: Executable compliance could replace conventional advisory deliverables
kp.d: Asked by Pollins about delivering advice through dashboards or visual tools, Shapiro says he has not done so. Instead, he proposes delivering operational code that implements a client's legal requirements, such as sales-tax compliance across all 50 states, rather than an explanatory memo. This is a prospective idea; Pollins raises unresolved boundaries between legal advice and software engineering and responsibility for incorrect code.
qs: I asked Zack whether he's started vibecoding things as a way of delivering advice. Dashboards, interactive maps, visual tools. His answer was no.
Not a memo about sales tax rules, but the code to make their sales engine compliant across all 50 states.
It's an interesting provocation, though it raises its own questions about where legal advice ends and software engineering begins, and who's responsible when the code is wrong.

kp.k: Privilege risks depend on confidentiality and counsel's direction
kp.d: Shapiro distinguishes the reported February 2026 Heppner ruling by Judge Rakoff in the Southern District of New York from law-firm enterprise AI use. The article describes a criminal defendant independently using consumer Claude under a policy permitting training on inputs, with no reasonable expectation of confidentiality and no privilege found. Shapiro argues that counsel-directed enterprise use with training disabled is different; Pollins explicitly leaves future judicial treatment unresolved.
qs: In Heppner, a criminal defendant used a consumer version of Claude, on his own initiative and not at counsel's direction, to research legal strategy.
The privacy policy allowed training on inputs. Judge Rakoff found no reasonable expectation of confidentiality and no privilege.
A law firm using an enterprise AI tool with training turned off, generating attorney work product at counsel's direction, is a different posture in Zack's view.
Whether the courts will draw that line clearly remains to be seen; Judge Rakoff himself noted that the analysis "might differ" if counsel had directed the AI use.

kp.k: Confidentiality requires case-specific choices, including withholding data
kp.d: The article presents data confidentiality as a case-by-case judgment rather than a universally solved issue. Options include zero-retention cloud hosting, custom DPAs, local inference, encrypted AI, and excluding certain information from models altogether.
qs: On data confidentiality: more nuanced, and requiring case-by-case judgment.
The spectrum runs from cloud-hosted with zero data retention, through custom DPAs, local inference, and encrypted AI, to simply not putting certain data into any model.

kp.k: Direct lawyer adoption competes with managed vendor platforms
kp.d: Shapiro criticizes some legal AI vendors for exploiting fear and selling expensive, restrictive workflows that he believes ultimately seek to automate their lawyer customers. He recommends that lawyers engage directly with technology and ethical obligations and build their own tools. Pollins qualifies this criticism by acknowledging that managed platforms may be some firms' practical compliance choice.
qs: He believes there are companies pushing expensive platforms with checkbox workflows that, in his view, ultimately aim to automate away the lawyers buying them.
He'd rather lawyers engage with the ethical rules and the technology directly and build things themselves.
Not everyone will agree; some firms will conclude that a managed platform is the most practical way to meet their compliance obligations, but Zack believes that is more fear and hype than reality.

kp.k: Lower prices combine discounted rates with reported AI efficiencies
kp.d: Shapiro reports that Rains charges hourly rates roughly half those of Big Law, with total service costs about a quarter because of additional AI-driven efficiencies. Most clients use subscriptions capped in human hours but intended to function as all-you-can-eat arrangements. Flat subscriptions are a long-term goal, conditional on improved reliability; these are firm-reported pricing claims rather than independently measured comparisons.
qs: Zack tells me that Rains charges hourly rates at roughly half the cost of Big Law, with overall service costs landing at about a quarter, the additional reduction coming from AI-driven efficiency.
Most clients are on subscriptions denominated in a cap of human hours but calculated to be functionally all-you-can-eat.
The long-term goal is flat subscriptions, but the technology isn't reliable enough yet to remove the human-attention safeguard.

kp.k: Human judgment and verification constrain subscription capacity
kp.d: Shapiro argues that AI weakens the connection between production hours and work-product value without eliminating the human time needed for judgment. He identifies overextension as a risk because it creates pressure to stop checking AI output, making human-attention limits a safeguard rather than merely a pricing convention.
qs: The tension Zack identifies is that the value of the work product is becoming untethered from the hours spent producing it, but the capacity to exercise judgment is still measured in human time.
Overextending means falling into the temptation of not checking the AI's output.

kp.k: AI may substitute for teams, not unlimited client judgment
kp.d: Rains reportedly runs multiple Claude chat and Cowork sessions concurrently. Shapiro believes one lawyer with Claude can replace a partner and associates on certain matters, but separates that task capacity from client growth: each additional client still needs human judgment. Expansion would require recruiting lawyers who work with AI as he does, whom he regards as scarce.
qs: Rains already runs multiple Claude chat and Cowork sessions in parallel (all on screen for now!)
In his opinion, one lawyer plus Claude can replace a partner plus a team of associates on certain matters.
But taking on more clients doesn't scale the same way, because each one requires human judgment.
To grow that side, he'd need to hire lawyers who use AI the way he does. That's a small pool right now.

kp.k: Competing futures involve platform dependence or direct professional adoption
kp.d: Shapiro considers training larger firms, forward deployment into in-house teams, and potentially selling his agentic workflow to a technology company. He frames the profession's future as a choice between process-driven, opinionated platforms and lawyers using AI directly to open up professional practice. These are contemplated business directions and scenarios, not established outcomes.
qs: He's thinking about what comes next: training for larger firms, forward deployment into in-house teams, possibly selling his agentic workflow to a tech company.

He sees two possible futures for the profession. One where everyone ends up inside opinionated platforms and everything becomes a process. Another where lawyers use AI directly and the profession opens up.

kp.k: Venture funding may incentivize automating judgment itself
kp.d: Pollins reports that Y Combinator's latest batch included AI-native law firms General Legal and LegalOS and legal service platform Arcline. Shapiro is not rushing to accept venture funding because he believes its incentives encourage automating judgment and degrading quality. He favors good lawyers supported by automation, invokes Atrium's $75 million raise and 2020 collapse as a cautionary example, and argues that available tools let him continue building without $60 million, while remaining open to conversations.
qs: Y Combinator's latest batch included two AI-native law firms: General Legal, and LegalOS, and another legal service platform, Arcline.
His concern is that the incentives of a venture-backed AI law firm push towards automating everything, including the judgment, and delivering what he bluntly believes is slop.
In his view, you need good lawyers doing the lawyering, with automation built around that.
He points to Atrium, the hybrid law firm and legal tech company that raised $75 million before imploding in 2020, as a cautionary tale.
He doesn't need $60 million to keep building skills. But he's open to conversations.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Shapiro describes AI as already changing document production, the economics of a small practice and staffing requirements, while leaving human judgment and verification as constraints on expansion.
pts.d:
1. Document production and context: Shapiro reports that Claude can manipulate Word documents directly, including tracked changes, rather than merely suggest edits for manual application. He believes local markdown files provide external memory that addresses context-window limitations in long-running work.
2. Reusable expertise: Shapiro argues that lawyers can encode judgment and successful instructions into reusable Skills files, distributing them at software-like scale. He identifies precise prompting and context, rather than additional model training or retrieval of templates, as the principal bottleneck. Iteratively updating Skills makes their usefulness compound. Pollins endorses experimentation with Skills but questions whether all practitioners have the time or inclination for this discipline.
3. Day-to-day work: Shapiro reports moving substantive legal work into Claude, generating engagement letters from brief instructions and eliminating much of the drudgery. He also describes a custom Claude Code–ElevenLabs document-reading tool that accommodates his difficulty reading long documents on screen.
4. Deliverables: Shapiro proposes moving beyond memos or visual summaries toward outputs that implement the client's objective—for example, code making a sales engine compliant across 50 states. This is a proposed direction, not a reported service he already delivers. Pollins raises boundary and responsibility questions when legal advice becomes software.
5. Pricing: Shapiro reports Rains' hourly rates at roughly half BigLaw's and total service costs at roughly a quarter, attributing the additional reduction to AI efficiency. Most clients have subscriptions capped by human hours but intended to function as all-you-can-eat. He aims eventually to offer flat subscriptions. He argues that work-product value is becoming detached from production hours, while judgment still consumes human time.
6. Staffing and growth: Shapiro believes one lawyer using Claude can replace a partner and associate team on certain matters. However, adding clients still requires human judgment and therefore recruitment of lawyers with comparable AI-working skills, whom he describes as scarce.
7. Confidentiality and privilege: Shapiro argues that counsel-directed enterprise AI use with training disabled differs from the consumer AI use described in Heppner. He does not present privilege protection as settled. He describes confidentiality decisions as case-specific, with options ranging from cloud arrangements to local or encrypted AI, or excluding some data entirely.
8. Market structure: Shapiro criticises some legal-AI vendors as selling fear through expensive, prescribed workflows that he believes ultimately seek to automate away their lawyer customers. He presents two possible professional futures: platform-controlled processes or direct lawyer use of AI that opens up the profession. Pollins notes that some firms may nevertheless find managed platforms the most practical compliance route.
9. Investment incentives: Shapiro argues that venture-backed AI law firms face pressure to automate judgment as well as tasks, risking poor-quality output. His preferred model retains good lawyers exercising judgment with automation around them. He argues that existing tools let him continue building Skills without a very large capital raise.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The principal evidence is Shapiro's account of his own practice; the article also invokes a privilege ruling and a failed legal-services venture, but supplies no independent productivity or quality benchmark.
pts.d: The operational claims rest on Shapiro's reported experience using Claude, Claude Code, local context files, reusable Skills and parallel sessions at Rains. Concrete illustrations include engagement-letter production, tracked-change document editing and a document-reading tool. The pricing ratios and subscription structure are practice-level reports, without an accompanying dataset, methodology, time records or independent comparison. The claim that a lawyer plus Claude can replace a partner and associate team is expressly presented as Shapiro's opinion, not a measured staffing outcome. His criticism of model-training/template approaches and his claim that usefulness compounds likewise derive from his experience and argument rather than benchmark results. The article reports that Rains has advised over 200 clients, but does not identify this as an AI-specific outcome sample. For privilege, Shapiro relies on his distinction between the February 2026 Heppner circumstances and counsel-directed enterprise use; Pollins reports that the judge left open whether counsel's direction would change the analysis. The ruling is a legal case offered to support a distinction, not a technical safety evaluation. Shapiro invokes Atrium's $75 million raise and 2020 collapse as a cautionary analogy for venture-funded hybrid legal businesses; the article does not establish that AI automation of judgment caused that failure. The implemented-code deliverable, alternative professional futures and investment-incentive claims are proposals or forecasts without systematic supporting evidence in the document. The post's 7.7 million views establish reported reach, not the effectiveness of the workflows.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Operational and pricing claims describe practice as of March 2026; broader changes are undated possibilities conditioned on disciplined use, reliable technology and retained human oversight.
pts.d: The article is dated 14 March 2026. Document automation, Skills, parallel Claude sessions, reported cost reductions and capped subscriptions are described as current practices. Their effectiveness is conditioned on precise instructions, substantial context and repeated refinement; Shapiro often writes prompts of about 2,000 words. Pollins explicitly questions whether that investment is feasible for every practitioner. Staffing substitution is limited to 'certain matters' and is not a claim that all legal work or whole firms can be automated. Client growth remains constrained by human judgment and the present scarcity of similarly skilled lawyers. Flat subscriptions are a long-term goal with no date: Shapiro says current reliability does not justify removing human-attention safeguards. Verification must remain feasible, since overextension creates pressure to leave outputs unchecked. Privilege protection for enterprise use is a conditional legal position, not a guarantee; relevant conditions include counsel's direction and disabling training, and the judicial distinction remains unresolved. Confidentiality measures depend on the particular data and matter. Implemented-code advice and the two professional futures have no specified adoption horizon. Shapiro is not presently rushing to accept venture funding but remains open to discussions.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The direct setting is a small corporate and startup-oriented practice; the projected effects extend to BigLaw staffing, corporate buyers, legal-AI vendors and venture-backed legal-service providers.
pts.d: Rains and comparable small practices are portrayed as able to increase matter-handling capacity without proportionate associate hiring, while retaining lawyer judgment and output checking. Lawyers may spend less time on document mechanics and experience more enjoyable work, but must invest in context preparation and iterative workflow development. Shapiro's reading tool also illustrates an individual accessibility benefit. Partners and associates at larger firms are affected by his proposed substitution of one AI-enabled lawyer for a traditional matter team; the article does not quantify profession-wide job losses or predict that all associate roles disappear. Rains' clients in corporate law, venture financing, digital assets and AI are the immediate beneficiaries of the reported lower costs and subscription arrangements. Corporate clients could also receive directly implementable compliance code rather than explanatory documents, although responsibility for faulty code remains a question raised by Pollins. BigLaw and in-house legal teams are prospective recipients of Shapiro's training or workflow deployment; these are contemplated opportunities, not completed engagements reported here. Legal-tech vendors selling software are the targets of his criticism of restrictive platforms, while venture-backed AI-native law firms are separately discussed as legal-service businesses subject to investor incentives. Confidentiality and privilege choices affect both lawyers and their clients. The article does not connect these enterprise service-cost claims to the unmet civil legal needs of individuals or small organisations.
